fr:mainmatter.html:p: I'm hoping to use Forester as a single place to manage a knowledge base, personal website, reference management a la Zotero, and daily research journal.
Some of these features are clunky so far, but I think it has great potential.

html:ul.html:li: Poor customization. The theming is decoupled from the Forester backend, which is likely a good thing. Although ideally this would be declaratively managed all in the toml

Ideally there would be a native way to decouple public from private. Apparently that is coming soon, but for the moment it is likely easier to just keep my research journal local instead of synced to my website
Is there a way to statically lock certain trees behind a key/password, and then store this as a cookie? I don't remember enough at the moment to be sure if this requires a true dynamic site
Reference management could likely use some niceties as well

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Subsets A of a set X may classically be identified with a characteristic map \chi _{A} : X \to \mathsf {bool}. Intuitively, for every x : X, \chi _{A} gives a truth value to the statement "x is in the subset A". In this manner, the domain of the characteristic map, \mathsf {bool}, classifies the subsets of X.
Generalizing over this principle, in a category \mathcal {C} an object \Omega is a subobject classifier if maps into it from some object c likewise uniquely identify a subobject of c.

We can understand \Omega to behave like an object of truth values that are not necessarily boolean valued. A morphism p : c \to \Omega can be thought of like a predicate on c. If c were a set, this would precisely be the characteristic function on it. However, this idea can generalize beyond sets. For instance in the category of graphs, \Omega is a cleverly constructed graph such that any graph homomorphism g \to \Omega into it picks out a unique subgraph of g.

There are always two (suggestively named) disjoint "points" of \Omega , thought of as morphisms out of the [terminal object]{sss-001O} \mathsf {true} , \mathsf {false} : \top \to \Omega . I think if we're being careful, \mathsf {true} may properly be the "subobject classifier" but I always use the term to refer to \Omega itself.
